replacement.title: Screen from the goalie’s sightline
replacement.objective: Choose a net-front position that affects the goalie’s view while leaving a passing lane
replacement.briefing: Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. D2 has the puck at the right point. YOU are above the crease, W is low far side, and Gold 1 fronts the shooting lane.
cues: D2 has the puck at the right point.
Gold 1 stands between D2 and the goalie; YOU are above the crease.

YOU leave D2 a visible lane

Move if Gold 1 seals the lane

questions.prompt: How can you screen without turning the play into a collision?
questions.explanation: Stay in the sightline while giving W and D2 separate routes, then move when Gold 1 closes your space; if the lane disappears, re-support.

questions.prompt: Who owns the puck after the short pass?
questions.explanation: The puck is assigned to F2 below the dot, so YOU must find a new support angle; if F2 loses it, the offensive read ends.

questions.prompt: Which two details should shape your reoffer?

options.text: The old wall spot staying unchanged

questions.explanation: F2’s location and Gold 1’s response determine the return lane; repeating the old spot can leave the pass behind pressure.

questions.prompt: Arrange one give-and-go reoffer.

options.text: Move to a new passing angle
Offer only if the lane stays visible

questions.explanation: Control tells you whether F2 can use support; the new angle changes the lane; a visible lane keeps the reoffer useful.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a wider support position with a different return angle from F2.
questions.explanation: The target changes width and sits below F2, creating a different return angle; it does not move closer to centre ice, and Gold 1 can still close it.

questions.prompt: If Gold 1 steps into the new return lane, what is a sensible next read?

options.text: Whether W or D2 is now clearer support
Whether to pass into Gold 1’s stick
Whether support is no longer needed

questions.explanation: Gold 1 is the visible defender who can remove the new return, so scan W and D2; if neither is available, F2 can protect and wait.

questions.prompt: How do you know your second movement improved the play?
questions.explanation: It should give F2 a visible option away from Gold 1 without crowding W or D2; if it only follows the puck and closes another lane, reset.

questions.prompt: From which side is Gold 1 closing?
questions.explanation: Gold 1’s inside approach is the pressure cue, so YOU can protect toward the wall and look for F2; a different approach would change the turn.

questions.prompt: Which two checks help before turning with the puck?

options.text: D2’s distance from the blue line

questions.explanation: The pressure side tells you where to place your body and F2 tells you whether a release exists; D2’s point position is far from this puck battle and does not solve the immediate pressure from Gold 1.

questions.prompt: Order one protective turn.

options.text: Place your body between pressure and puck
Use F2 only if the lane is clear

questions.explanation: The pressure read chooses the protective side; body position buys time; F2 becomes useful only when the pass lane is visible.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a side-lane support position while keeping F2 in the scan.
questions.explanation: The target changes the side-lane angle relative to Gold 1 and F2; it is not on the boards, and facing does not prove a glance or sightline.

questions.prompt: If F2 becomes clearly available below you, what might help?

options.text: A short protected pass into F2’s visible lane
Turning away from both puck and support

questions.explanation: F2’s clear lane converts protection into possession; if F2 is covered again, continue protecting or use D2.

questions.prompt: What makes a protective turn useful in this scene?
questions.explanation: The turn moves the puck away from Gold 1 while keeping a reachable support lane, giving YOU time to choose; if no support opens, protection is safer than surrendering the puck.

questions.prompt: Which attacker is inside?
questions.explanation: Gold 1 carries through the middle, so the inside lane is first; if the carrier moves wide, the picture changes.

questions.prompt: Which two checks matter before closing?

options.text: Whether D1 will automatically stop the inside pass

questions.explanation: The carrier’s lane and D1’s support determine how you close without giving up middle; noise does not describe the rink.

questions.prompt: Arrange one inside-first gap read.

options.text: Keep the carrier outside your body line

questions.explanation: The route sets priority; steering outside protects the net-side lane; the second scan updates pass and recovery options.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to an inside position between Gold 1 and the Navy net.
questions.explanation: The target is inside Gold 1 relative to the defended net, but it is not a centre-ice claim; if Gold 2 cuts inside, include D1’s help.

questions.prompt: If Gold 2 cuts toward the middle, what should YOU reconsider first?

options.text: Whether D1 can take Gold 2 while YOU contains Gold 1
Chasing the puck and losing both lanes

questions.explanation: Gold 2’s cut creates a coverage decision, so communicate and keep the carrier from the net; if D1 cannot help, stay inside the most dangerous lane.

questions.prompt: Why is the drawn distance alone insufficient for an exact gap?
questions.explanation: The useful gap depends on carrier speed, support and passing lane, which can change after the freeze; if those cues change, closing distance changes too.
